items.stem: Paper 1 – Question (a). Define the term "secondary source". [2]
items.answer: A source that interprets or analyses primary evidence, such as a news analysis or an academic review
items.markingKey: A source that interprets or analyses primary evidence, such as a news analysis or an academic review. 2 marks for a clear definition that includes the defining feature; 1 mark for a partial or vague definition.

items.stem: Paper 1 – Question (a). Define the term "algorithm". [2]
items.answer: A finite, ordered set of unambiguous instructions for solving a problem or completing a task
items.markingKey: A finite, ordered set of unambiguous instructions for solving a problem or completing a task. 2 marks for a clear definition that includes the defining feature; 1 mark for a partial or vague definition.

items.stem: Paper 1 – Question (b). Explain why algorithmic bias can be more harmful than individual human bias. [4]
items.answer: An algorithm applies the same biased rule consistently to thousands or millions of cases, often invisibly and with an appearance of objectivity, making the harm larger and harder to detect and challenge.
items.markingKey: An algorithm applies the same biased rule consistently to thousands or millions of cases, often invisibly and with an appearance of objectivity, making the harm larger and harder to detect and challenge. Award up to 4 marks: 1 mark per relevant point, up to 2 further marks for developing the explanation (cause → effect) and for a relevant example.

items.stem: Paper 1 – Question (b). Explain why the variety of big data creates challenges for analysis. [4]
items.answer: Data comes in many forms – text, images, sensor readings, transactions – often unstructured and from different sources, so it must be cleaned, combined and interpreted, which is complex and can introduce errors.
items.markingKey: Data comes in many forms – text, images, sensor readings, transactions – often unstructured and from different sources, so it must be cleaned, combined and interpreted, which is complex and can introduce errors. Award up to 4 marks: 1 mark per relevant point, up to 2 further marks for developing the explanation (cause → effect) and for a relevant example.

items.stem:
Paper 1 – Question (c). Real-world example: The Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai volcanic eruption in January 2022 cut Tonga's single international undersea cable, leaving the country largely offline for about five weeks.

Analyse how this example illustrates dependence on network infrastructure. [6]
items.answer: A single physical link meant one event disconnected a whole country, showing the vulnerability of networks without redundancy.
items.markingKey: A single physical link meant one event disconnected a whole country, showing the vulnerability of networks without redundancy. 5–6: analysis that links specific features of the example to the concept and considers impacts on more than one stakeholder; 3–4: relevant explanation, partly developed; 1–2: description of the example with little analysis.

items.stem:
Paper 1 – Question (c). Real-world example: From 2023–24 very large platforms in the EU must explain the main parameters of their recommender systems and offer a feed not based on profiling (e.g. TikTok and Instagram added chronological or non-personalised feeds in the EU).

Analyse how this example illustrates regulation for transparency. [6]
items.answer: Requiring explanations and alternatives gives users some insight and choice, without forcing companies to publish code.
items.markingKey: Requiring explanations and alternatives gives users some insight and choice, without forcing companies to publish code. 5–6: analysis that links specific features of the example to the concept and considers impacts on more than one stakeholder; 3–4: relevant explanation, partly developed; 1–2: description of the example with little analysis.

items.stem: Paper 1 – Question (d). "Algorithm audits make automated hiring fair." Using a specific real-world example, discuss this view. [8]
items.answer: Audits improve visibility of bias but do not by themselves guarantee fairness without obligations to act and independent oversight.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: measure disparities such as impact ratios; public summaries create pressure to improve. Arguments against: audits may only test limited groups and metrics; no obligation to change the tool (NYC LL144); auditors may be paid by the employer. Possible conclusion: Audits improve visibility of bias but do not by themselves guarantee fairness without obligations to act and independent oversight. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: Paper 1 – Question (d). With reference to a real-world example you have studied, evaluate the claim that sensor data from smart devices does more good than harm. [8]
items.answer: Benefits are significant where data is minimised, secured and used for clear purposes; without these safeguards, the privacy harms can outweigh them.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: efficiency in energy, transport and health monitoring; early warning (air quality, falls in elderly people). Arguments against: continuous monitoring reveals routines and habits; security weaknesses in IoT devices; data used for insurance or marketing without clear consent. Possible conclusion: Benefits are significant where data is minimised, secured and used for clear purposes; without these safeguards, the privacy harms can outweigh them. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem:
Paper 2 – Question 1. Read Source C.

Source C
"Platforms do not just host speech; they decide what gets seen. That is a form of power no newspaper editor ever had over billions of people."
— Technology policy researcher, interview with a European broadcaster, 2021

Identify two ways in which platforms exercise power according to Source C. [2]
items.answer: deciding what content gets seen (ranking/visibility); reaching/controlling billions of people at once
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to 2 marks: deciding what content gets seen (ranking/visibility); reaching/controlling billions of people at once. Points must come from the source; accept close paraphrase.

items.stem:
Paper 2 – Question 2. Read Source B.

Source B
"By clicking Accept All, you agree to the use of cookies by us and our 847 partners. You can change your preferences at any time."
— Cookie consent banner on a European news website, 2024

Explain how Source B relates to the GDPR requirement for consent. [4]
items.answer: The GDPR requires consent that is freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous; a banner pushing "Accept all" for 847 partners makes genuinely informed choice unrealistic, which regulators have criticised.
items.markingKey: The GDPR requires consent that is freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous; a banner pushing "Accept all" for 847 partners makes genuinely informed choice unrealistic, which regulators have criticised. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit reference to the source; 1–2 marks: limited explanation or quotation without explanation.

items.stem:
Paper 2 – Question 3. Read Sources B and C.

Source B
"We have 4G on the hill now, but a smartphone costs two months of my wages and data runs out in a week."
— Farmer in rural Malawi, interviewed for a 2023 study on connectivity

Source C
"Every school connected by 2030."
— Mission of Giga, a joint initiative of UNICEF and the ITU launched in 2019

Compare and contrast what Source B and Source C reveal about how the digital divide might be closed. [6]
items.answer: Similarities: both concern rural or underserved populations. Differences: Source B suggests cost is the main barrier; Source C proposes infrastructure/connectivity for schools; B is a user perspective; C is an organisational goal.
items.markingKey: Similarities: both concern rural or underserved populations. Differences: Source B suggests cost is the main barrier; Source C proposes infrastructure/connectivity for schools; B is a user perspective; C is an organisational goal. 1 mark per valid, source-referenced point (up to 6). If only similarities or only differences are given, maximum 3 marks. Reward a running comparison.

items.stem:
Paper 2 – Question 4. Read Sources B and C.

Source B
"Aadhaar has saved the government tens of thousands of crore rupees by removing ghost and duplicate beneficiaries, and has given more than a billion residents a verifiable identity for the first time."
— Statement attributed to a senior official of the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI), 2019

Source C
"Platforms do not just host speech; they decide what gets seen. That is a form of power no newspaper editor ever had over billions of people."
— Technology policy researcher, interview with a European broadcaster, 2021

Using the sources and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that organisations that control digital systems are accountable for how they use their power. [12]
items.answer: Supporting: courts and regulators can intervene (Puttaswamy, DMA); oversight bodies such as Meta's Oversight Board. Challenging: algorithmic decisions are opaque (Source C); official sources may downplay harms (Source B); affected people have little voice (Source A).
items.markingKey: Supporting: courts and regulators can intervene (Puttaswamy, DMA); oversight bodies such as Meta's Oversight Board. Challenging: algorithmic decisions are opaque (Source C); official sources may downplay harms (Source B); affected people have little voice (Source A). Markbands [12]: 10–12 – sustained, balanced evaluation that integrates the sources/stimulus with specific own knowledge and Digital Society concepts, and reaches a well-supported conclusion; 7–9 – evaluation with relevant evidence and some balance; 4–6 – some analysis, mostly descriptive or one-sided; 1–3 – limited, general points with little evaluation. Responses that use only the sources or only own knowledge cannot reach the top band.

items.stem:
Paper 3 – Question 1. Read the extract from the intervention brief.

From July 2023, employers in New York City using automated employment decision tools must commission an independent bias audit every year, publish the selection rates and impact ratios by sex and race/ethnicity, and tell candidates that such a tool is used.

Explain the challenge that New York City Local Law 144 is intended to address. [4]
items.answer: Employers increasingly use automated tools to screen CVs and interviews, and evidence (e.g. Amazon's abandoned tool) showed such systems can reproduce discrimination invisibly at scale.
items.markingKey: Employers increasingly use automated tools to screen CVs and interviews, and evidence (e.g. Amazon's abandoned tool) showed such systems can reproduce discrimination invisibly at scale. 1 mark for identifying the challenge; up to 3 marks for explaining its causes and who is affected, with reference to the extract.

items.stem:
Paper 3 – Question 2. Read the extract from the intervention brief.

The DPDP Act requires data fiduciaries to obtain consent for processing digital personal data, sets up a Data Protection Board and allows penalties of up to ₹250 crore. It also lets the central government exempt state agencies from its provisions.

Analyse the impact of India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 on two different stakeholders. [6]
items.answer: citizens – new rights to information, correction and erasure; businesses and start-ups – compliance duties and penalties; government agencies – broad possible exemptions; civil-society groups – concerns about surveillance and independence of the Board
items.markingKey: Possible stakeholder impacts: citizens – new rights to information, correction and erasure; businesses and start-ups – compliance duties and penalties; government agencies – broad possible exemptions; civil-society groups – concerns about surveillance and independence of the Board. Up to 3 marks per stakeholder: identification (1), analysis of the impact (1), link to the extract or own knowledge (1).

items.stem:
Paper 3 – Question 3. Read the extract from the intervention brief.

The EU AI Act (in force 2024) classifies AI used in recruitment, credit scoring, education and law enforcement as high-risk. Providers must manage risks, use quality data, keep logs, ensure human oversight and register systems before use; fines can reach €15 million or 3% of turnover for breaches of these duties.

Evaluate the EU AI Act's rules for high-risk AI systems as a response to this challenge and recommend one further step that could improve it. [12]
items.answer: Provide clear technical standards and regulatory sandboxes for small firms, and give affected individuals an accessible complaints route.
items.markingKey: Strengths: binding, risk-based obligations before deployment; EU-wide market influence (Brussels effect); human oversight and logging enable accountability. Limitations: complex and slow to implement (phased to 2026–27); standards still being developed; exemptions for national security. Possible recommendation: Provide clear technical standards and regulatory sandboxes for small firms, and give affected individuals an accessible complaints route. Markbands [12]: 10–12 – sustained, balanced evaluation that integrates the sources/stimulus with specific own knowledge and Digital Society concepts, and reaches a well-supported conclusion; 7–9 – evaluation with relevant evidence and some balance; 4–6 – some analysis, mostly descriptive or one-sided; 1–3 – limited, general points with little evaluation. A recommendation must be justified with reference to stakeholders and feasibility for the top band.

items.stem: Paper 1 – Question (a). Define the term "political expression". [2]
items.answer: Communicating views about power, government and public issues, for example through hashtags, livestreams or online petitions
items.markingKey: Communicating views about power, government and public issues, for example through hashtags, livestreams or online petitions. 2 marks for a clear definition that includes the defining feature; 1 mark for a partial or vague definition.

items.answer: An output that wrongly fails to flag something that is present, such as a fraudulent transaction that is missed

items.stem: Paper 1 – Question (b). Explain why a source's purpose affects its value for an inquiry. [4]
items.answer: A source created to persuade or sell may select favourable evidence and omit costs, so it is valuable for showing a stakeholder's perspective but limited as evidence of actual impacts.
items.markingKey: A source created to persuade or sell may select favourable evidence and omit costs, so it is valuable for showing a stakeholder's perspective but limited as evidence of actual impacts. Award up to 4 marks: 1 mark per relevant point, up to 2 further marks for developing the explanation (cause → effect) and for a relevant example.

items.stem: Paper 1 – Question (b). Explain why metadata can reveal as much about a person as the content of their communications. [4]
items.answer: Metadata shows who contacted whom, when, where and how often; patterns over time reveal relationships, routines, health concerns or political links without reading any content, which is why intelligence agencies collect it in bulk.
items.markingKey: Metadata shows who contacted whom, when, where and how often; patterns over time reveal relationships, routines, health concerns or political links without reading any content, which is why intelligence agencies collect it in bulk. Award up to 4 marks: 1 mark per relevant point, up to 2 further marks for developing the explanation (cause → effect) and for a relevant example.

items.stem:
Paper 1 – Question (c). Real-world example: In 2020 school closures affected over 1.5 billion learners worldwide (UNESCO), and many systems moved lessons to video-conferencing and learning platforms.

Analyse how this example illustrates how impacts differ between stakeholders. [6]
items.answer: Students with devices and broadband continued learning, while those without access fell behind, showing that the same digital system had unequal impacts and long-term implications for educational inequality.
items.markingKey: Students with devices and broadband continued learning, while those without access fell behind, showing that the same digital system had unequal impacts and long-term implications for educational inequality. 5–6: analysis that links specific features of the example to the concept and considers impacts on more than one stakeholder; 3–4: relevant explanation, partly developed; 1–2: description of the example with little analysis.

items.stem:
Paper 1 – Question (c). Real-world example: India stores Aadhaar biometric and demographic data in a central database managed by UIDAI.

Analyse how this example illustrates centralised data storage and security. [6]
items.answer: Centralising data on over a billion people makes services efficient but creates a high-value target, so security failures could have national consequences.
items.markingKey: Centralising data on over a billion people makes services efficient but creates a high-value target, so security failures could have national consequences. 5–6: analysis that links specific features of the example to the concept and considers impacts on more than one stakeholder; 3–4: relevant explanation, partly developed; 1–2: description of the example with little analysis.

items.stem: Paper 1 – Question (d). "Algorithms make fairer decisions than humans." Using a specific real-world example, discuss this view. [8]
items.answer: Algorithms can be more consistent, but fairness depends on design, data and oversight; they are not inherently fairer than humans.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: consistent rules applied to everyone; not affected by mood, fatigue or personal prejudice. Arguments against: learn and reproduce historical bias (Ofqual 2020, COMPAS); opaque and hard to challenge; consistency can spread one error to thousands of people. Possible conclusion: Algorithms can be more consistent, but fairness depends on design, data and oversight; they are not inherently fairer than humans. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: Paper 1 – Question (d). With reference to a real-world example you have studied, evaluate the claim that memes have become one of the most powerful forms of political communication. [8]
items.answer: Memes are influential for framing and identity, especially among young people, but their power is hard to measure and often works alongside other media.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: memes spread quickly and reach young audiences; they simplify complex issues and build group identity. Arguments against: simplification can spread misinformation; impact on actual votes or policy is hard to prove; traditional media and campaigns still dominate agenda-setting. Possible conclusion: Memes are influential for framing and identity, especially among young people, but their power is hard to measure and often works alongside other media. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem:
Paper 2 – Question 1. Read Source C.

Source C
"Freedom of speech and expression through the medium of internet is an integral part of Article 19(1)(a)... an order suspending internet services indefinitely is impermissible."
— Supreme Court of India, Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India, January 2020

Identify two points made by the court in Source C. [2]
items.answer: expression through the internet is constitutionally protected (Article 19(1)(a)); indefinite suspension of internet services is not permitted
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to 2 marks: expression through the internet is constitutionally protected (Article 19(1)(a)); indefinite suspension of internet services is not permitted. Points must come from the source; accept close paraphrase.

items.stem:
Paper 2 – Question 2. Read Source C.

Source C
"Unexplained algorithms should not decide who goes to prison."
— Statement by a civil-liberties organisation following State v. Loomis, 2016

Explain the perspective expressed in Source C. [4]
items.answer: It argues that when liberty is at stake, defendants must be able to understand and challenge evidence; secret, unexplained scores undermine due process.
items.markingKey: It argues that when liberty is at stake, defendants must be able to understand and challenge evidence; secret, unexplained scores undermine due process. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit reference to the source; 1–2 marks: limited explanation or quotation without explanation.

items.stem:
Paper 2 – Question 3. Read Sources A and B.

Source A
"Facebook users who had downloaded the app gave it permission to access their friends' data as well. Of the estimated 87 million people affected, only around 270,000 had installed the app themselves."
— Summary of evidence to the UK Parliament's Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee, 2018

Source B
"By clicking Accept All, you agree to the use of cookies by us and our 847 partners. You can change your preferences at any time."
— Cookie consent banner on a European news website, 2024

Compare and contrast what Source A and Source B reveal about consent to the use of personal data. [6]
items.answer: Similarities: both show consent obtained in ways users may not understand; both involve many third parties receiving data. Differences: Source A describes data taken from people who never consented at all; Source B describes a consent request that exists but is hard to understand; A is a past scandal; B is current routine practice.
items.markingKey: Similarities: both show consent obtained in ways users may not understand; both involve many third parties receiving data. Differences: Source A describes data taken from people who never consented at all; Source B describes a consent request that exists but is hard to understand; A is a past scandal; B is current routine practice. 1 mark per valid, source-referenced point (up to 6). If only similarities or only differences are given, maximum 3 marks. Reward a running comparison.

items.stem:
Paper 2 – Question 4. Read Sources B and C.

Source B
"We have 4G on the hill now, but a smartphone costs two months of my wages and data runs out in a week."
— Farmer in rural Malawi, interviewed for a 2023 study on connectivity

Source C
"Every school connected by 2030."
— Mission of Giga, a joint initiative of UNICEF and the ITU launched in 2019

Using the sources and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that improving infrastructure is the most effective way to close the digital divide. [12]
items.answer: Supporting: many people still lack coverage, especially in rural areas; school connectivity (Source C) gives shared access. Challenging: coverage exists but devices and data are unaffordable (Source B); skills and relevant content also matter; gender norms limit women's access.
items.markingKey: Supporting: many people still lack coverage, especially in rural areas; school connectivity (Source C) gives shared access. Challenging: coverage exists but devices and data are unaffordable (Source B); skills and relevant content also matter; gender norms limit women's access. Markbands [12]: 10–12 – sustained, balanced evaluation that integrates the sources/stimulus with specific own knowledge and Digital Society concepts, and reaches a well-supported conclusion; 7–9 – evaluation with relevant evidence and some balance; 4–6 – some analysis, mostly descriptive or one-sided; 1–3 – limited, general points with little evaluation. Responses that use only the sources or only own knowledge cannot reach the top band.

items.stem:
Paper 3 – Question 1. Read the extract from the intervention brief.

In 2018 WhatsApp limited forwarding in India to five chats at once and labelled forwarded messages; in 2020 it limited "highly forwarded" messages to one chat at a time, saying this reduced such forwards by 70%.

Explain the challenge that WhatsApp's message-forwarding limits is intended to address. [4]
items.answer: False rumours spread rapidly through private, encrypted group chats and were linked to mob violence, but end-to-end encryption meant the platform could not read or moderate the messages.
items.markingKey: False rumours spread rapidly through private, encrypted group chats and were linked to mob violence, but end-to-end encryption meant the platform could not read or moderate the messages. 1 mark for identifying the challenge; up to 3 marks for explaining its causes and who is affected, with reference to the extract.

items.stem:
Paper 3 – Question 2. Read the extract from the intervention brief.

From December 2024 the EU requires phones, tablets, cameras, headphones and other small devices sold in the EU to use USB-C charging, with laptops following in 2026, and allows devices to be sold without a charger.

Analyse the impact of the EU common charger law on two different stakeholders. [6]
items.answer: consumers – reuse chargers and save money; manufacturers such as Apple – had to switch from Lightning ports; environment – less charger e-waste; accessory makers – standardised market
items.markingKey: Possible stakeholder impacts: consumers – reuse chargers and save money; manufacturers such as Apple – had to switch from Lightning ports; environment – less charger e-waste; accessory makers – standardised market. Up to 3 marks per stakeholder: identification (1), analysis of the impact (1), link to the extract or own knowledge (1).

items.stem:
Paper 3 – Question 3. Read the extract from the intervention brief.

In 2018 WhatsApp limited forwarding in India to five chats at once and labelled forwarded messages; in 2020 it limited "highly forwarded" messages to one chat at a time, saying this reduced such forwards by 70%.

Evaluate WhatsApp's message-forwarding limits as a response to this challenge and recommend one further step that could improve it. [12]
items.answer: Combine friction with in-app fact-checking tips (e.g. search-the-web button), partnerships with local fact-checkers and digital-literacy campaigns.
items.markingKey: Strengths: design change preserves end-to-end encryption and privacy; measurable reduction in viral forwards; simple, global and low-cost. Limitations: rumours still spread through many small forwards and other apps; does not address content already shared; cannot distinguish harmful from useful content. Possible recommendation: Combine friction with in-app fact-checking tips (e.g. search-the-web button), partnerships with local fact-checkers and digital-literacy campaigns. Markbands [12]: 10–12 – sustained, balanced evaluation that integrates the sources/stimulus with specific own knowledge and Digital Society concepts, and reaches a well-supported conclusion; 7–9 – evaluation with relevant evidence and some balance; 4–6 – some analysis, mostly descriptive or one-sided; 1–3 – limited, general points with little evaluation. A recommendation must be justified with reference to stakeholders and feasibility for the top band.

items.stem: Paper 1 – Question (a). Outline what is meant by "Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)" in the context of digital society. [2]
items.answer: International guidelines from the W3C for making web content accessible, organised around four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable and robust
items.markingKey: International guidelines from the W3C for making web content accessible, organised around four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable and robust. 2 marks for a clear definition that includes the defining feature; 1 mark for a partial or vague definition.

items.stem: Paper 1 – Question (a). Define the term "malware". [2]
items.answer: Malicious software such as viruses, worms, trojans, spyware and ransomware designed to damage systems or steal data
items.markingKey: Malicious software such as viruses, worms, trojans, spyware and ransomware designed to damage systems or steal data. 2 marks for a clear definition that includes the defining feature; 1 mark for a partial or vague definition.

items.stem: Paper 1 – Question (b). Explain why people may present different identities on different platforms. [4]
items.answer: Each platform has different audiences and norms (LinkedIn professional, Instagram curated, Finsta/private accounts informal), so people manage impressions by selecting what to show, as Goffman's idea of performance suggests.
items.markingKey: Each platform has different audiences and norms (LinkedIn professional, Instagram curated, Finsta/private accounts informal), so people manage impressions by selecting what to show, as Goffman's idea of performance suggests. Award up to 4 marks: 1 mark per relevant point, up to 2 further marks for developing the explanation (cause → effect) and for a relevant example.

items.stem: Paper 1 – Question (b). Explain why predictive policing systems can create feedback loops. [4]
items.answer: If police are sent where the algorithm predicts crime, they record more crime there, which is fed back as training data, so the system predicts even more crime in the same areas – reinforcing existing patterns regardless of actual crime rates.
items.markingKey: If police are sent where the algorithm predicts crime, they record more crime there, which is fed back as training data, so the system predicts even more crime in the same areas – reinforcing existing patterns regardless of actual crime rates. Award up to 4 marks: 1 mark per relevant point, up to 2 further marks for developing the explanation (cause → effect) and for a relevant example.

items.stem:
Paper 1 – Question (c). Real-world example: ProPublica's 2016 "Machine Bias" investigation of the COMPAS recidivism tool in Broward County found that Black defendants who did not reoffend were almost twice as likely as white defendants to be labelled higher risk; Northpointe disputed the analysis.

Analyse how this example illustrates algorithmic bias in criminal justice. [6]
items.answer: Unequal false positive rates meant the costs of errors fell disproportionately on Black defendants, influencing bail and sentencing decisions.
items.markingKey: Unequal false positive rates meant the costs of errors fell disproportionately on Black defendants, influencing bail and sentencing decisions. 5–6: analysis that links specific features of the example to the concept and considers impacts on more than one stakeholder; 3–4: relevant explanation, partly developed; 1–2: description of the example with little analysis.

items.stem:
Paper 1 – Question (c). Real-world example: Edward Snowden leaked NSA documents showing bulk collection of phone metadata and the PRISM programme accessing data from companies such as Google, Facebook and Apple.

Analyse how this example illustrates state mass surveillance. [6]
items.answer: Governments had built population-wide surveillance using commercial platforms, prompting legal changes (USA Freedom Act 2015) and wider use of encryption.
items.markingKey: Governments had built population-wide surveillance using commercial platforms, prompting legal changes (USA Freedom Act 2015) and wider use of encryption. 5–6: analysis that links specific features of the example to the concept and considers impacts on more than one stakeholder; 3–4: relevant explanation, partly developed; 1–2: description of the example with little analysis.

items.stem: Paper 1 – Question (d). "Responsibility for limiting the harms of the attention economy lies with users, not platforms." Using a specific real-world example, discuss this view. [8]
items.answer: Users have some responsibility, but because platforms design and profit from engagement, they and regulators (e.g. design codes, the DSA) carry the greater responsibility.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: users can set limits, turn off notifications and choose alternatives; digital citizenship emphasises personal responsibility. Arguments against: platforms deliberately design for compulsive use; children and teenagers are especially vulnerable; information asymmetry means users cannot see how design manipulates them. Possible conclusion: Users have some responsibility, but because platforms design and profit from engagement, they and regulators (e.g. design codes, the DSA) carry the greater responsibility. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: Paper 1 – Question (d). With reference to a real-world example you have studied, evaluate the claim that the environmental costs of digital technology outweigh its environmental benefits. [8]
items.answer: Digital technology can support sustainability, but only if its own footprint is managed through renewable energy, longer device lifetimes and recycling.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: e-waste, mining and data-centre energy; rapidly rising AI electricity demand. Arguments against: smart grids, remote working and dematerialisation can cut emissions; environmental monitoring by satellites and sensors; efficiency gains (PUE improvements). Possible conclusion: Digital technology can support sustainability, but only if its own footprint is managed through renewable energy, longer device lifetimes and recycling. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

Paper 2 – Question 3. Read Sources B and C.

Source B
"Aadhaar has saved the government tens of thousands of crore rupees by removing ghost and duplicate beneficiaries, and has given more than a billion residents a verifiable identity for the first time."
— Statement attributed to a senior official of the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI), 2019

Source C
"Platforms do not just host speech; they decide what gets seen. That is a form of power no newspaper editor ever had over billions of people."
— Technology policy researcher, interview with a European broadcaster, 2021

Compare and contrast what Source B and Source C reveal about power held by organisations that run digital systems. [6]
items.answer: Similarities: both describe organisations with influence over very large populations; both imply control over access (to welfare or to visibility). Differences: Source B presents this power as beneficial and administrative; Source C presents it as a concern; B is about state power; C is about private platform power.
items.markingKey: Similarities: both describe organisations with influence over very large populations; both imply control over access (to welfare or to visibility). Differences: Source B presents this power as beneficial and administrative; Source C presents it as a concern; B is about state power; C is about private platform power. 1 mark per valid, source-referenced point (up to 6). If only similarities or only differences are given, maximum 3 marks. Reward a running comparison.

items.stem:
Paper 2 – Question 4. Read Sources A and B.

Source A
"Black defendants who did not reoffend were nearly twice as likely as white defendants to be misclassified as higher risk (45% versus 23%)."
— ProPublica, "Machine Bias" investigation of COMPAS in Broward County, Florida, 2016

Source B
"Our analysis shows the tool is equally accurate for Black and white defendants: a given score means the same probability of reoffending in each group."
— Summary of Northpointe's response to ProPublica, 2016

Using the sources and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that algorithmic risk-assessment tools make criminal justice fairer. [12]
items.answer: Supporting: consistent scores may reduce individual judges' inconsistency; tool is calibrated across groups (Source B). Challenging: unequal false positive rates (Source A); proprietary and unexplained (Loomis); historical arrest data embeds bias.
items.markingKey: Supporting: consistent scores may reduce individual judges' inconsistency; tool is calibrated across groups (Source B). Challenging: unequal false positive rates (Source A); proprietary and unexplained (Loomis); historical arrest data embeds bias. Markbands [12]: 10–12 – sustained, balanced evaluation that integrates the sources/stimulus with specific own knowledge and Digital Society concepts, and reaches a well-supported conclusion; 7–9 – evaluation with relevant evidence and some balance; 4–6 – some analysis, mostly descriptive or one-sided; 1–3 – limited, general points with little evaluation. Responses that use only the sources or only own knowledge cannot reach the top band.

items.stem:
Paper 3 – Question 1. Read the extract from the intervention brief.

Giga, launched in 2019, maps schools and their connectivity, and works with governments and companies to finance internet connections for schools. It reports having connected thousands of schools and millions of students, but many countries still have large numbers of unconnected schools.

Explain the challenge that Giga, the UNICEF–ITU school connectivity initiative is intended to address. [4]
items.answer: Hundreds of millions of children attend schools without internet access, limiting their access to information and digital skills and widening inequality between and within countries.
items.markingKey: Hundreds of millions of children attend schools without internet access, limiting their access to information and digital skills and widening inequality between and within countries. 1 mark for identifying the challenge; up to 3 marks for explaining its causes and who is affected, with reference to the extract.

items.stem:
Paper 3 – Question 2. Read the extract from the intervention brief.

Giga, launched in 2019, maps schools and their connectivity, and works with governments and companies to finance internet connections for schools. It reports having connected thousands of schools and millions of students, but many countries still have large numbers of unconnected schools.

Analyse the impact of Giga, the UNICEF–ITU school connectivity initiative on two different stakeholders. [6]
items.answer: students – access to online learning and skills; teachers – new resources but need for training; governments – need sustainable funding for ongoing costs; telecom providers – new contracts and markets
items.markingKey: Possible stakeholder impacts: students – access to online learning and skills; teachers – new resources but need for training; governments – need sustainable funding for ongoing costs; telecom providers – new contracts and markets. Up to 3 marks per stakeholder: identification (1), analysis of the impact (1), link to the extract or own knowledge (1).

items.stem:
Paper 3 – Question 3. Read the extract from the intervention brief.

From April 2024 the UK banned default or easily guessable passwords on consumer connected devices, required manufacturers to publish a way to report vulnerabilities and to state how long security updates will be provided.

Evaluate the UK Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure (PSTI) regime as a response to this challenge and recommend one further step that could improve it. [12]
items.answer: Extend requirements to minimum update periods and coordinate with the EU Cyber Resilience Act to raise global standards.
items.markingKey: Strengths: tackles the most common weakness (default passwords); clear, simple requirements; transparency about update periods helps consumers choose. Limitations: enforcement against online marketplaces and imports is difficult; only basic security covered; existing devices unaffected. Possible recommendation: Extend requirements to minimum update periods and coordinate with the EU Cyber Resilience Act to raise global standards. Markbands [12]: 10–12 – sustained, balanced evaluation that integrates the sources/stimulus with specific own knowledge and Digital Society concepts, and reaches a well-supported conclusion; 7–9 – evaluation with relevant evidence and some balance; 4–6 – some analysis, mostly descriptive or one-sided; 1–3 – limited, general points with little evaluation. A recommendation must be justified with reference to stakeholders and feasibility for the top band.
